raw_case_text:
A 16-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with complaints of dizziness, syncope, weakness, and fatigue. He was drowsy and had a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, pulse rate of 20 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 95%. He was febrile with a temperature of 37.7 C. Systemic examination was unremarkable, and his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15/15. An urgent electrocardiogram (EKG) showed complete AV dissociation and ST segment depressions in leads I, II, and avL (Figure 1(a)). Atropine 1 mg IV was given, and an infusion of normal saline was started for hemodynamic support. A repeat ECG did not show any improvement. No history of using rate-limiting drugs was found. Subsequently, the patient was transferred to the cardiac cath lab, and a temporary pacemaker (transvenous) was placed. A paced rhythm was achieved, and the rate was set to 75 bpm (Figure 1(b)). The patient improved after that. Further history revealed that 6 days ago, the patient was taken to another hospital due to continuous high-grade fever, severe body aches, and an episode of epistaxis. He had stable vital signs. Apart from routine investigations, dengue serology was ordered which came out positive. There he was treated with IV paracetamol, antibiotics, and fluids. The patient refused hospital admission and was sent home on symptomatic treatment and necessary advice. We performed serial investigations that are shown in Table 1.
His dengue IgM was again positive, and confirmatory dengue polymerase chain reaction showed DENV-2 serotype. The patient was commenced on IV antipyretics, IV cefoperazone-sulbactam 2 g twice daily, and fluids. Platelets were transfused due to low platelets count and an episode of epistaxis and hematemesis on one occasion. Serial troponin-I, CK-MB, ESR, CRP, and LDH levels remained persistently elevated. The patient's blood culture, malarial antigen, typhoid serology, influenza virus, COVID-19, and diphtheria testing were negative. During hospitalization, he experienced only mild shortness of breath but no chest pain. His ejection fraction, systolic function, and valve anatomy were normal with no evidence of congenital heart disease on the echocardiogram (Figure 2). Based on the ECG findings and unusual cardiac enzymes changes, a clinical diagnosis of dengue myocarditis with CHB was made. A cardiac MRI was in the plan but contraindicated due to the temporary pacemaker (TPM) in place, so it could not be done. The family refused an endomyocardial biopsy. The patient remained TPM dependent for 1 week (Figure 1(c)) with no return of normal spontaneous rhythm. Ultimately, it was decided to place a permanent pacemaker. Unfortunately, the night before the surgery, the patient collapsed suddenly and died despite resuscitative efforts.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with dizziness, syncope, weakness, and fatigue following a 6-day history of high-grade fever, severe body aches, and epistaxis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six days prior to presentation, the patient was evaluated at another hospital for continuous high-grade fever, severe body aches, and an episode of epistaxis; dengue serology was positive, and he received intravenous paracetamol, antibiotics, and fluids before declining admission and returning home on symptomatic therapy. He subsequently presented to our emergency department with dizziness, syncope, weakness, and fatigue. During hospitalization, he also experienced one episode of epistaxis and hematemesis and mild shortness of breath without chest pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of congenital heart disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, severe body aches, weakness, fatigue, dizziness, syncope, epistaxis, hematemesis (one episode during hospitalization), and mild shortness of breath. Pertinent negatives: no chest pain; no history of taking rate-limiting medications.

objective.physical_examination: On presentation, the patient was drowsy and febrile (temperature 37.7 °C) with a pulse rate of 20 bpm, blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 95%, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15. Systemic physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Urgent ECG showed complete atrioventricular (AV) dissociation (complete heart block) and ST-segment depressions in leads I, II, and aVL, with no improvement after 1 mg intravenous atropine. Serial laboratory investigations demonstrated thrombocytopenia, persistently elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin-I, CK-MB, LDH), and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP). Dengue IgM serology was positive. Blood culture, malarial antigen, typhoid serology, influenza virus, COVID-19, and diphtheria testing were all negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal ejection fraction, normal systolic function, and normal valve anatomy without congenital heart disease.
objective.advanced_workup: Confirmatory dengue RT-PCR identified DENV-2 serotype. Transvenous temporary pacemaker (TPM) was placed in the cardiac catheterization laboratory (set at 75 bpm). Cardiac MRI was planned but contraindicated due to the temporary pacemaker in situ, and the family declined endomyocardial biopsy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Dengue myocarditis complicated by complete heart block (CHB), confirmed by positive dengue IgM serology, confirmatory DENV-2 PCR, characteristic ECG showing complete AV dissociation, and persistently elevated troponin-I and CK-MB. Typhoid fever, malaria, bacterial sepsis, influenza, COVID-19, and diphtheria were ruled out. Initial emergency management included IV atropine (1 mg), normal saline infusion, emergent transvenous temporary pacemaker placement (achieving a paced rhythm at 75 bpm), IV antipyretics, IV cefoperazone-sulbactam 2 g twice daily, IV fluids, and platelet transfusions for thrombocytopenia with epistaxis and hematemesis. The patient remained pacemaker-dependent after 1 week without recovery of spontaneous rhythm and was scheduled for permanent pacemaker implantation; however, the night before surgery, he suffered a sudden collapse and died despite resuscitative efforts.
